cues.text: A Physician Formed by Faith
Born on October 4, 1922, at Magenta, near Milan, Gianna Beretta was the tenth of thirteen children in a devoutly Catholic family.
She grew up combining serious academic study with active charitable service among the elderly and needy as a member of the Society of St. Vincent de Paul.
She earned degrees in medicine and surgery from the University of Pavia in 1949, then specialized further in pediatrics.

She opened a clinic near Milan, giving particular attention to mothers, infants, the poor, and the elderly—a practice she understood from the outset as an extension of her faith rather than separate from it.
She had once hoped to offer her medical skills as a missionary in Brazil alongside her own brother, a priest.
However, her own delicate health made such distant service impossible, and she turned her gifts instead to pediatric medicine closer to home.
A Marriage of Shared Joy

Gianna married the engineer Pietro Molla in September 1955, and their surviving correspondence during their engagement, later published, reveals a couple who saw ordinary married love itself as a genuine path to holiness.

Three children followed in quick succession — Pierluigi, Mariolina, and Laura — and Gianna continued her medical practice throughout, balancing her professional vocation with the demands of a growing family with evident, unforced joy.
Their surviving letters show two people who understood from the beginning that the ordinary joys of married life — a shared home, children, daily work — were themselves a genuine vocation.
They understood this vocation as asked of them by God, as fully as any more visibly religious calling.
A Difficult Pregnancy
In September 1961, early in a fourth pregnancy, Gianna was found to have a fibroma in her uterus requiring surgical removal.
Her surgeons recommended a complete hysterectomy, which would have ended the pregnancy.
Gianna consented only to removal of the tumor itself, unwilling to accept a procedure that would directly end her child's life.
Instead, she accepted whatever risk to her own health the more limited surgery might carry.
"Save the Baby"
As the pregnancy continued under increasing medical difficulty, Gianna made her wishes plain to her husband and family.
If a choice ever had to be made between her own life and the child's, they were to save the child without hesitation.
On Holy Saturday, April 21, 1962, her daughter, also named Gianna, was delivered safely by Caesarean section.

In the days that followed, however, Gianna Beretta Molla developed septic peritonitis, and despite every effort of her physicians, she died at home a week later, on April 28, 1962, at only thirty-nine years old.
A Mother, Not a Martyr of the Delivery Room
The Church has been careful to note that Gianna was not canonized for having died in childbirth.
Her death came from post-operative infection rather than the delivery itself.

She was canonized for the consistent, deliberate integrity of a choice made months earlier: refusing a procedure that would have taken her child's life directly, and accepting whatever consequence that refusal might bring for her own.
It is this quiet, sustained fidelity — not a single dramatic moment, but months of steady resolve — that the Church holds up for imitation.
Doctors and family alike understood, even before her death, the gravity of the choice she had made months earlier.
What followed was not a single dramatic sacrifice in the delivery room, but the working-out, over painful weeks, of a decision already fully and freely given.
Legacy
Gianna was beatified on April 24, 1994, and canonized on May 16, 2004, both by Pope John Paul II.
Her husband Pietro and youngest daughter were present at both ceremonies—the first time a spouse had ever witnessed his own wife’s canonization.
Honored today as patroness of mothers, physicians, and unborn children, Gianna Beretta Molla remains a witness to the total gift of self.
The Gospel asks this of every believer.
It can be lived out as fully in an ordinary medical practice and a happy marriage as in any convent, so long as love, once given, is never withdrawn when the cost of keeping it becomes clear.
